name: environment-design-getting-started
description: "Use on first run with a new owner: onboard them one question at a time, list what they provide, and run the first Environment Design Director grade with the lens engine."
---

> **Audit contract v1 (overrides everything below).** Created by @meta_alchemist (https://x.com/meta_alchemist).
> - Score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-11-environment-design v1.2.0). `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` computes the grade; this skill only gathers evidence for it and never adds points of its own.
> - Missing evidence is UNMEASURED (0 points, not a defect). A test that did not run is NOT_RUN, never PASS. Never invent a measurement; label every worked example synthetic.
> - Game facts and budgets come from your game profile (`pack.profile`). Treat sample numbers as illustrative. Set the frame-time budget separately for each target device in your game profile.
> - An automated gate needs a negative fixture that fails. Receipts carry measured values, never an unconditional PASS.
> Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

# Environment Design Director: Getting Started

Review placement, sightlines and visual cues so players can identify landmarks and navigate the spaces in your game.

It works for any view: a 2D side-scroller, a top-down or isometric map, a 3D third-person or first-person world, a race track or a puzzle board. Every example below is one case among several; use only what fits the owner's game.

If `engine/lens.mjs`, `engine/lens-kit.mjs` or `fixtures/good-pack.json` are not on disk yet, write them byte for byte from the `environment-design-lens-engine` skill first (Node 18+, no dependencies).

## 1. Onboard one question at a time

Ask one question at a time, wait for the answer, then ask the next. Never stack questions in one message. Give no setup steps until questions 2 and 3 are answered.

1. Which game are we reviewing, and what kind of spaces does it have (levels, rooms, a town, a world map, tracks or a board)? After the answer, ask for the build to review (a build ID, commit or version), then ask where the evidence will come from (a CI job, an editor script or manual captures).
2. How does the player see the world: a 2D side view, top-down, isometric, a 3D third-person or first-person camera, or a fixed screen? Use only examples that match this view from now on. If players do not move through spaces (for example a card table or a fixed puzzle board), agree with the owner which route lines stay U (often `traversal-affordance:2` and `camera-occlusion:1`); a "route" can also be the order of moves on the board.
3. Which engine or level tool builds the scenes (for example Unity, Unreal, Godot, Tiled or LDtk for tile maps, or a custom editor)? Do not install tools or change project settings on your own.
4. Which things must the player always be able to see along a route? For example the next ledge, a door, the goal, an enemy, a pickup, the finish line or the next valid move.
5. Which objects can the player use, stand on or hide behind, and which are only decoration? The rubric line `traversal-affordance:1` checks that players can tell these apart. If the world has no usable objects at all, leave the line U.
6. Does the game show location names or area cards over play (a banner that names an area, a region card or a map pop-up)? If not, we use the `no-location-overlays` profile: `visual-navigation:2` reads N/A, not U, and `visual-navigation:1` takes the pillar's 20 points. If yes, in which moments must they stay out of the way, for example a boss fight, a timed jump, a puzzle's final move, a race's last lap or a dialogue choice? These moments become `overlayStates`.
7. Which values go in your game profile (`pack.profile`)? Start from the synthetic profile in `fixtures/good-pack.json` and go through the keys in the table below one at a time. Confirm or replace each value; never keep a sample number without the owner saying so.
8. Who will judge the five visual lines (for example an art director, a level designer or a small playtest panel)?
9. Who reviews the local finding drafts?

| Profile key | What it means |
|---|---|
| `minLandmarkPx` | Smallest on-screen size, in pixels, at which a landmark (a tower, a big tree, a coloured door, a lighthouse) must still be recognisable. |
| `landmarkDevice` | The device or screen class where that size is checked, usually the smallest one you support. |
| `overlayStates` | The game states where location overlays are observed and must not cover anything critical. |
| `maxOccludedCueFrames` | How many frames a needed cue may be hidden by scenery along a test route. |
| `devices`, `maxArtDeltaE` | The devices compared for colour consistency, and the largest colour difference allowed between them. DeltaE is a standard colour distance; about 2 is barely visible. |

Read the profile pick back to the owner and, once they approve, set it before scoring: `"rubricProfile": ["no-location-overlays"]` in `pack.profile`. Name it next to the grade. The route and usable-object lines in questions 2 and 5 have no profile: when they do not apply they stay U and the verdict stays CONDITIONAL; say so in the report.

Before grading a real pack, check that its build and profile match what the owner chose. Record a capture or run that could not happen as NOT_RUN. Each computed line needs a sample population (the list of measured cases it reads); `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` lists them.

## 2. What you provide

- An evidence pack (JSON) with `status: "VALID"`, a `liveSha` (the build that was running when you captured), a `gitSha` (the source commit) and a `packId` (all three are required), and an `artifacts` list. Every metric group names the artifact id it came from.
- Metric groups this engine reads: `landmarks` (capture), `locationOverlays` (trace; the location overlays), `occlusionProbe` (trace), `occlusion` (capture), `consistency` (capture).
- Profile thresholds in `pack.profile`. A missing threshold makes its line U, never a default.
- Judgements for the five visual lines (`scene-composition:1`, `scene-composition:2`, `traversal-affordance:1`, `traversal-affordance:2`, `environment-consistency:1`): `pack.judgements["<line id>"] = { level, judge, evidenceIds, note }`. The judge is a named person or panel, and every evidence id must be a capture in the pack.
- Anything you cannot capture yet stays out of the pack. It grades U (UNMEASURED), which is honest and costs no false defect. With `no-location-overlays` approved, leave `locationOverlays` out; that line reads N/A. Any other line your game does not need has no profile and stays U.

## 3. Run the first grade

```
node engine/lens.mjs fixtures/good-pack.json   # worked example, synthetic, not a measurement
node engine/lens.mjs your-pack.json            # your build
node engine/lens.mjs --meta                    # rubric lines, weights and what each reads
node engine/lens.mjs --fixtures fixtures/good-pack.json  # negative and missing-input self-test
```

Read the record: `verdict` (PASS, CONDITIONAL, BLOCKED or INVALID), `grade` and `coverage`, then each line's `level` and `findings`, then `checks` (growth checks reported beside the grade) and `tickets` (deduplicated candidates).

## 4. Report in plain English

- Lead with the verdict, grade and coverage in one sentence. Say how much of the rubric was measured.
- List U lines as "not measured yet" with the capture that would measure them. Never call them defects.
- One local ticket draft per measured finding, with the pack id and artifact ids. Label any synthetic pack as synthetic.
- Rubric lines: visual-navigation:1, visual-navigation:2, scene-composition:1, scene-composition:2, camera-occlusion:1, camera-occlusion:2, traversal-affordance:1, traversal-affordance:2, environment-consistency:1, environment-consistency:2.

## 5. Skills in this template

- `environment-set-dressing-and-grounding-director`: Place decorative detail so players can recognize landmarks, tell usable objects from decoration and read the intended routes, in 2D or 3D.
- `placement-and-support-surface-auditor`: Check that placed objects rest on the surface they belong on (floor, tile, shelf, terrain) and follow the project's placement rules.
- `sightline-silhouette-and-value-composition-gate`: Check whether important objects and actions stay readable from the cameras and routes players actually use.
- `entry-scene-optional-interactions`: If your game has a title, menu or hub scene with decorative objects, design optional reactions for them and check that players can still find and use the main action.
- `environment-design-lens-engine`: the engine source and how to run it.

## Blockers to tell the owner about

- Five lines are visual judgements and stay U until a named judge records them with real captures.

For the five judged lines, collect route captures in bright, dark and busy scenes (for example a night level, a crowded market or a screen full of effects). Mark usable surfaces, decorative objects and hidden cues, and note the version of the art reference.

Before capture, agree on the test cases in `profile.cases`: for `camera-occlusion:1`, one case per route and camera with its seed and whether the target should be visible. After capture, `receipts.sightlines` holds one measured row per case with the case id, the `liveSha` of the build that ran, the trace artifact id and the measured values. Run `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` for the required row fields and comparisons. A skipped or stale case leaves its line U. The bundled rows and budgets are synthetic.

name: environment-set-dressing-and-grounding-director
description: "Place decorative detail so players can recognize landmarks, tell usable objects from decoration and read the intended routes, in 2D or 3D."
---

> **Audit contract v1 (overrides everything below).** Created by @meta_alchemist (https://x.com/meta_alchemist).
> - Score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-11-environment-design v1.2.0). `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` computes the grade; this skill only gathers evidence for it and never adds points of its own.

Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

# Place and ground scene detail

Set dressing means placing the detail objects that make a space feel real (crates, plants, signs, furniture, debris) around the playable layout. Done well, it points players toward where to go and what they can use. Done badly, it hides the route or makes decoration look usable. This skill feeds the judged lines `scene-composition:2`, `traversal-affordance:1`, `traversal-affordance:2` and `environment-consistency:1`, and the computed line `visual-navigation:1`.

## 0. Ask first

Ask how the player sees the world (2D side view, top-down, isometric, 3D third-person, first-person or a fixed board) and which tool builds the scenes. Then use only the matching checks:

- 2D side view or top-down: check layer order, foreground overlap, silhouettes against the background and tile edges.
- Isometric: check draw order around tall objects and whether objects behind walls stay readable.
- 3D: check contact points, scale, perspective and what the camera sees at player height.

If the game has no free movement (for example a fixed-screen puzzle or a card game), only the composition parts apply: keep decoration from competing with the pieces the player acts on, and leave the route lines U.

## 1. Plan before detail

Mark the player's route, camera positions and decision points (forks, jumps, doors, shop counters, the next puzzle piece) before adding detail. Use scale, grouping, local contrast and empty space to draw the eye toward each decision.

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- 2D platformer: foreground vines frame the screen but never overlap the ledge the player must land on.
- Top-down RPG village: a tall well and a red-roofed inn act as landmarks; small barrels never block a doorway.
- Farming or life sim: crops and fences read as usable, while flower pots read as decoration.
- Racing game: trackside banners and cones lean into the next turn and stay outside the racing line.
- Turn-based strategy game: terrain props show which tiles block movement and which are only scenery.
- 3D arena or exploration game: crates that can be climbed share one look; decorative rubble looks different.

## 2. Fit and ground

Fit each object to its support surface and intended material: no floating crates, no chairs half inside a wall. Keep decorative collision separate from walkable geometry unless the design calls for an obstacle. Sample views at the approach, the decision point and the exit, including the smallest supported display.

## 3. Compare and prove

Compare captures with the approved art reference. For the judged lines, give the named judge annotated captures and record their call as `pack.judgements["<line id>"] = { level, judge, evidenceIds, note }`. In a test copy, deliberately lift a grounded object or cover a route cue and verify that the review catches it.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `environment-design-lens-engine`). If the scene or tool is not available, record NOT_RUN.

skills.name: placement-and-support-surface-auditor
skills.description: Check that placed objects rest on the surface they belong on (floor, tile, shelf, terrain) and follow the project's placement rules.
skills.content:

name: placement-and-support-surface-auditor
description: "Check that placed objects rest on the surface they belong on (floor, tile, shelf, terrain) and follow the project's placement rules."
---

> **Audit contract v1 (overrides everything below).** Created by @meta_alchemist (https://x.com/meta_alchemist).
> - Score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-11-environment-design v1.2.0). `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` computes the grade; this skill only gathers evidence for it and never adds points of its own.

> - Game facts and budgets come from your game profile (`pack.profile`). Treat sample numbers as illustrative. Set the frame-time budget separately for each target device in your game profile.
> - An automated gate needs a negative fixture that fails. Receipts carry measured values, never an unconditional PASS.
> Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

# Inspect support surfaces

Check that every placed object rests on the surface it belongs on, with no corner floating over an edge and no base sunk into the ground. A support surface is whatever an object should stand on: a floor, a tile, a shelf, a table top, terrain or a road. No line in this template computes grounding by itself: the overlay you produce goes to the named judge for `environment-consistency:1` and `traversal-affordance:2`. For numeric foot and base gaps on single props, use `animation-and-weapon-clearance:2` in Prop & Rig Director (03).

## 0. Ask first

Ask which engine or level tool holds the scene, then use only the matching way to read world positions:

- Unity: each Transform's `localToWorldMatrix`, and `Physics.Raycast` down from each footprint sample.
- Unreal: the actor or instance transform, and a line trace down from each footprint sample.
- Godot: `global_transform`, and a ray query (`intersect_ray`) or a RayCast node for each sample.
- Tile maps (Tiled, LDtk, or the tile map node in Unity or Godot): the tile under each footprint cell and its tile type or tags.
- Three.js: an instance's world matrix is the object's `matrixWorld` multiplied by its local instance matrix. Transform the footprint by that product before testing contacts, and test one instance inside a rotated parent to catch coordinate-space mistakes.

If the scene format is not one you can read, record NOT_RUN and name the export the owner would need to provide. Do not install tools on your own.

## 1. Sample the footprint

Expand instanced or batched geometry into world-space positions, keyed by a stable object or instance ID (use the instance or batch ID when the object has no name). Sample each footprint at its corners, along its edges and across the interior, scaled to the object. A centre-point test alone misses a corner floating over an edge. For large scenes, use the engine's spatial index before precise tests.

Compare contact depth, slope and material tags with the project's placement rules (the allowed surfaces and the largest allowed gap, agreed with the owner). Bridges, steps and intentional overhangs need explicit expected values.

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- 2D platformer: a crate placed half over a one-way platform edge, so it hovers when the tile below is removed.
- Top-down RPG: a market stall straddling a road tile and a water tile.
- City or racing game: a bin sitting half on the pavement and half over a kerb edge, so one corner floats.
- Life sim: a lamp on a table that is placed slightly above the table top.
- Strategy game: a tree on a tile tagged as buildable, which contradicts the movement rules.

## 2. Classify and export

Given the world-space sample hits from the chosen adapter, classify the complete footprint before accepting the placement:

```js
function assessFootprint(samples, expectedCount, allowedMaterials, maxGap) {
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(expectedCount) || expectedCount < 1 || !Array.isArray(samples) ||
      samples.length !== expectedCount || !allowedMaterials.length || !Number.isFinite(maxGap)) return { status: "NOT_RUN" };
  const cells = new Set();
  const rejected = [];
  for (const sample of samples) {
    if (!sample || !Number.isFinite(sample.gap) || typeof sample.material !== "string") return { status: "NOT_RUN" };
    if (sample.cell == null || cells.has(sample.cell)) return { status: "NOT_RUN" };
    cells.add(sample.cell);
    if (!allowedMaterials.includes(sample.material)) rejected.push({ cell: sample.cell, reason: "material" });
    if (Math.abs(sample.gap) > maxGap) rejected.push({ cell: sample.cell, reason: "contact gap" });
  }
  return { status: rejected.length ? "FAIL" : "PASS", rejected };
}
```

Export a support grid, an annotated overlay of the outliers and a rejection reason per object ID. Use a synthetic or local scene for the worked example.

## 3. Negative fixture

Include a deliberately misplaced object whose footprint crosses two incompatible surfaces (for example a floor tile and a ledge edge). The check must return FAIL for it.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `environment-design-lens-engine`).

# Check sightlines and composition

A sightline is the clear line of view from the player's camera to something they need to see. Composition is how the scene arranges shapes, light and dark so the eye goes to the right place. "Value" here is the art term for how light or dark a colour is: a dark object on a light background reads even when the colours are similar. This skill feeds `camera-occlusion:1`, `camera-occlusion:2` and the judged line `scene-composition:1`.

## 0. Ask first

Ask how the player sees the world and which engine draws it, then use only the matching check:

- 2D side view: check overlap, layer order and foreground effects between the camera and the player or target.
- Top-down or isometric: check tall objects, roofs and tree canopies drawn over the player or a target, and whether they fade or cut away.
- 3D: cast rays from the camera to each target and check what geometry sits between them.
- Fixed board or screen: check that effects and decoration never cover the pieces or tiles the player acts on.

## 1. Pick the targets and routes

Name the focal point and the cues the player must see at each decision point (from the owner's answer during setup). Record normal and extreme camera views along each approved route.

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- 2D platformer: a foreground pillar hides the player for several frames while they line up a jump.
- Top-down action RPG: a tree canopy hides a pickup until the player is standing on it.
- Isometric strategy game: a tall building hides a unit standing behind it; the wall should cut away.
- 3D third-person adventure: the camera slides behind a column and the next ledge disappears.
- Racing game: a trackside billboard blocks the view of the next corner.
- Mobile puzzle game: a sparkle effect covers the tile the player needs to tap.
- 3D arena game: smoke or foliage hides an opponent's outline at a range the design says should be visible.

## 2. Measure

- `camera-occlusion:1`: export one versioned sightline trace (schema `sightline-v1`) per approved case, with the seed, route, camera, whether the target was visible by ray, whether it should be visible, and how many frames the cue was hidden. Store one row per case in `receipts.sightlines`. If another team or template also reads this trace (for example level design), record that use separately with its own artifact ID and build; if nobody else reads it yet, note the shared use as NOT_RUN.
- `camera-occlusion:2`: count frames on each test route where scenery hides a needed cue (`occlusion.routes`, `occlusion.occludedCueFrames`).
- `scene-composition:1`: capture bright, dark and busy versions of the scene (for example a night level, a crowded market or a screen full of effects) and give them to the named judge. Compare outline separation, light and dark contrast, and time obscured with the art reference.

If decorative geometry fades or cuts away, check that its collision still matches the design, so the player cannot walk through something that looks solid.

## 3. Negative fixture and review

Keep paired images with the focal point marked. In a test copy, place an object that blocks a required cue and confirm the check fails. Ask a reviewer to name the next action from a capture at the smallest intended display size.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `environment-design-lens-engine`). If the build or capture tool is not available, record NOT_RUN.

# Make an interactive entry scene

Use this only if your game has an entry scene: a title screen, main menu, lobby or hub where decorative objects sit around the main controls. If the entry is a plain menu with no scene behind it, skip this skill.

The goal is small optional reactions (a sign tilts when tapped, a cat looks at the cursor) that add charm without slowing the player down. The main action always wins.

## 0. Ask first

Ask, one at a time: what is the player's first task on this screen (for example continue a save, start a level, join a session or pick a puzzle)? Is the scene 2D or 3D, and which engine draws it? Which inputs does the game support (mouse, touch, controller, keyboard)? Then plan only for those answers.

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- 2D platformer title screen: a parallax forest; a bird hops when the cursor passes. Main action: Start.
- Mobile puzzle game: tiles on the start screen jiggle when tapped. Main action: Play, which must stay the largest tap target.
- Farming or life sim: a farmhouse porch; the mailbox wobbles on focus. Main action: Continue.
- Racing game: a garage; headlights flash when the car is focused. Main action: Race.
- Turn-based strategy game: a map table; flags sway on hover. Main action: Resume campaign.
- 3D menu scene: a shelf of collectibles; one spins when clicked. Main action: Play.

## 1. Design

Place optional interactions away from the main controls and keep focus order stable for every supported input (a controller or keyboard must reach the main action in the same number of steps as before). Choose one reaction that fits the art direction. Limit how many effects can run at once, release temporary audio and animation objects when they finish, and respect reduced-motion and mute settings.

Put the reactions behind a feature switch that is off by default. Before any decorative motion starts, check both the owner's opt-in and the current accessibility setting:

```js
function entranceMotion(ownerOptIn, enabled, reducedMotion) {
  return ownerOptIn === true && enabled === true && reducedMotion === false;
}
```

## 2. Measure

Compare, with and without the reactions: time to reach the main action, accidental activations of decorations, and worst-case frame time. Repeat on the smallest supported display. Test the switch when it is missing, set to an invalid value and set to off; each case must behave exactly like the baseline. Then test the switch on with reduced motion enabled and keep the paired captures.

Negative fixture: in a test copy, let a decorative object overlap the main button. The input check must fail because the decoration steals the tap or click.

## 3. Which rubric lines this feeds

No rubric line scores the entry scene on its own. When the owner lists the entry scene as one of the representative scenes in the game profile, its frame-time trace can count toward the full-scene budget line in Prop & Rig Director (`scene-budget:1`), and its focal-point captures can support the prop hierarchy judgement in Environment Design Director (`scene-composition:2`). Otherwise keep the results as a local review note: they do not change the grade, and nothing is filed or shared without the human.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` only for the lines named above. If the scene or build is not available, record NOT_RUN.

memory.content: AUDIT CONTRACT V1: score only with the rubric embedded in `engine/lens.mjs` (`LENS.rubric`, gbf-11-environment-design v1.2.0), 100 points, 5 pillars of 20, levels 0 to 4, pass at level 3. Grade with `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` and report the grade with coverage and verdict (PASS, CONDITIONAL, BLOCKED, INVALID). UNMEASURED earns 0 and is never a defect; N/A is excluded from averages. Review focus for this template: use the same sightline probe for level geometry and environment art. Trace a location overlay from its event to its on-screen result, and record the critical moments of your game (for example a timed jump, a puzzle's final move, a race's last lap or a boss fight).

ENGINE: the lens engine is embedded in the environment-design-lens-engine skill. Write both files byte for byte before the first run. Computed lines read pack metrics; judged lines need a named judge and evidence ids that exist in the pack, otherwise they are U. Computed lines trust pack.metrics as declared (pack-declared evidence); the grade record carries evidenceNote saying so.

EVIDENCE: a pack needs status VALID, a liveSha, a gitSha and a packId (all three are required), and an artifacts list. Metric groups read: landmarks, locationOverlays (location overlays), occlusionProbe, occlusion, consistency. Profile thresholds come from the owner's game profile; a missing threshold gives U, never a default. Check the sample populations listed by the engine in --meta. Empty evidence earns U. NOT APPLICABLE: the approved no-location-overlays profile (no location names or area cards over play) marks visual-navigation:2 N/A; the owner approves it before scoring and sets rubricProfile in the game profile, visual-navigation:1 takes the pillar's 20 points, the verdict can reach PASS, and the report names the profile. Any other line the game does not need (for example routes on a fixed board) has no profile: it stays U, the verdict stays CONDITIONAL, and it is never a defect.

ONBOARDING: ask one question at a time. Before suggesting any check, ask how the player sees the world (2D side view, top-down, isometric, 3D or a fixed board) and which engine or level tool builds the scenes, and use only examples that fit. Settle early: who judges the five visual lines (for example an art director, a level designer or a playtest panel), which cues must always stay visible, and when location overlays must stay out of the way; if the game shows no location names or area cards over play, the no-location-overlays profile, approved by the owner before scoring.

HOUSE RULES: use the frame-time and response targets for each supported device from the game profile. No en or em dashes. Write the game's full name. Credit @meta_alchemist. Label every worked example synthetic and never invent a measurement.

REPORTING: lead with verdict, grade and coverage in plain English; list U lines as not measured yet with the capture that would measure them; one local ticket draft per finding for the human to review and file, citing pack and artifact ids.
BLOCKERS: Five lines are visual judgements and stay U until a named judge records them with real captures.

Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

TEAM: this is gbf-11-environment-design version 2.0.1, team spec 1.0.0. Before acting, read inputs from .grokbot-team/artifacts/<artifact>/ (game-profile (required), evidence-pack (required), asset-budget-report, hud-capture-set) and memory topics decisions, releases from .grokbot-team/memory/. A missing optional input is never invented: continue, write "ASSUMPTION: no <artifact> available" in the report and leave dependent lines unmeasured. Save outputs (layout-brief, grade-record, ticket-draft) as local files for human review. Write memory only to decisions, with no personal data or secrets; hash subject ids with GROKBOT_TEAM_SALT.
